It is a habit of the Qur'an to seize the opportunity to renew admonition and reflection when souls' attachment to this world weakens, when they reflect on what comes after death, and when they lend their ears to the call to guidance. Thus they become prepared to accept the truth in the places where this is expected, though their readiness varies. How often has such seizing of the opportunity been the cause of faith in hard hearts. When God manifests the signs through the hand of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to confirm his truthfulness, He follows that with renewed reminder, as He says, ﴿And We do not send the signs except as a warning﴾ [al-Isra 17:59].

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold that this verse was revealed as a witness against the polytheists, through the manifestation of a great sign and one of the miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely the miracle of the splitting of the moon. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, he said: The people of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to show them a sign, so he showed them the splitting of the moon. Al-Tirmidhi adds, on the same authority: The moon was split in two in Mecca, and then there was revealed, ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ up to His words, ﴿a continuous magic﴾ [al-Qamar 54:2].

In the narration of al-Tirmidhi on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, he said: While we were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Mina, the moon split.

The apparent meaning of this is that it occurred during the season of the Hajj. In al-Sira al-Halabiyya, it is said that it happened on the fourteenth night, that is, in the last nights of Mina, the night of departure (al-nafr). In it, the polytheists gathered at Mina, among them al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-'As ibn Hisham, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ): If you are truthful, then split the moon for us into two halves. And the moon split.

The foundation of this interpretation rests on the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud in the Sahih, where he said: The moon split while we were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at Mina, and it split into two halves: a half above the mountain and a half below it. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to us: Bear witness, bear witness. In the narration of al-Tirmidhi on his authority, he said: meaning, ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾. I say: And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: half on Abu Qubays and half on Qu'ayqi'an.

The same has been related on the authority of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, Anas ibn Malik, and Jubayr ibn Mut'im. These did not witness the splitting of the moon, because all of them except 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar were not in Mecca and did not embrace Islam until after the Hijra. But they spoke only on the basis of certainty.

The large number of transmitters of this report indicates that it was a widely known report (khabar mustafid). In his commentary on al-Mawaqif, al-Iji said that it is mutawatir (mass-transmitted). There is looseness in his expression, since the conditions of tawatur are not fully met. What he means is that it is mustafid.

The apparent meaning of some of the narrations of the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in al-Tirmidhi is that the verse was revealed before the splitting of the moon in Mecca occurred, when the polytheists asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a sign, or they asked him to split the moon, and so he showed them the splitting of the moon. It occurs only when the Hour draws near. This was related from al-Hasan and 'Ata', and it is what is referred to by the eclipse in the surah of al-Qiyama: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled and the moon is eclipsed﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:7-8].

This does not contradict the occurrence of the splitting of the moon which the polytheists asked for, but it is not what is intended in this verse. Rather, it is to be interpreted in light of what is in its narration in sources other than al-Tirmidhi.

According to the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, the verse was revealed after the splitting of the moon.

In light of all these narrations, the splitting of the moon, which is a miracle, took place in this world. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, he said: Five have passed: al-Lizam, the Romans, the grasping, the moon, and the smoke. On the authority of al-Hasan and 'Ata', the splitting of the moon will occur at the Resurrection. This was chosen by al-Qushayri, and it was related from al-Balkhi. Al-Mawardi said: It is the view of the majority, but it is not known that this is the view of the majority.

The report of the splitting of the moon is counted among the topics of miracles in the books of the Sira and the proofs of prophethood.

The wording of this verse is not explicit that it occurred, but the apparent meaning of the verse necessitates it, as in al-Shifa' (of Qadi 'Iyad).

If the revelation of this verse took place after the splitting, as the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi requires, then beginning the surah with ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ is for the sake of emphasizing admonition, as we have mentioned just before, since the purpose of confirming the miracle has been established.

Thus that miracle was made a means of reminder of the nearness of the Hour by way of idmaj (embedding), on the basis that the moon is one of the celestial bodies, with an order that follows the order of the terrestrial atmosphere. When a change occurred in its order, which was not customary, it was appropriate to alert people to reflect on the possibility of the passing away of this world. The past tense verb is used in its literal sense. It has been related that Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman recited, ﴿and the moon has split﴾.

If the revelation of this verse was before the splitting, as the hadith of Anas ibn Malik requires, then it is a warning of the nearness of the Hour and the splitting of the moon, which is one of the signs of the Hour, with an allusion that the splitting will be a miracle in response to what the polytheists ask. This interpretation is supported by the next verse, ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾ [al-Qamar 54:2], as will come there.

Since most of the early exegetes and those after them have understood this verse to mean that the splitting of the moon occurred before its revelation or near its revelation, we must demonstrate the possibility of this splitting occurring, following the possibilities arising from the reports about the splitting, to refute the denial of the atheists and to make it easier for believers to understand.

It is possible that a great eclipse occurred in the sphere of the moon, which created in its face a crevice that appeared to observers in the form of a split into two halves with darkness between them, so that it seemed to be split into two moons. Thus the expression "splitting" corresponds to reality, since the crevice is a split, and it agrees with what people saw, since they saw it as if it were split.

It is also possible that between the direction of the moon and the direction of the sun, in the horizon, there passed a celestial body, from the direction of some comets, which blocked the light of the sun from the face of the moon to the extent of that body's shadow, in the manner of what is called a partial eclipse. There is nothing in the wording of the hadith of Anas ibn Malik in Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, or of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas in al-Bukhari, that contradicts this.

It is possible that the splitting was a composite event consisting of a half-eclipse of the moon in the usual manner of eclipses, which blocked half of the moon, while the moon was in the direction of one of the two mountains. At that time there was in the atmosphere a watery cloud in which the image of the moon, eclipsed, was reflected in the shine of its water, such that the observer saw another half of the moon not eclipsed, rising in the direction of that mountain. This is one of the strange events of the atmosphere. Similar events have been known with respect to the rays of the sun, and it is possible that similar ones occur with respect to the light of the moon, though this is extremely rare. We have mentioned this when discussing His words, ﴿And when We shook the mountain above them﴾ [al-A'raf 7:171] in the surah of al-A'raf.

This is supported by what al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of 'Ikrima, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The moon was eclipsed during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they said: The moon has been bewitched. Then ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ was revealed, up to the end of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas called it an eclipse, approximating its type.

This view does not contradict the splitting being a miracle, because its occurrence at the time when they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a sign, together with God's inspiration to them to ask for it at the moment of God's decree, is sufficient for it to be a sign of truthfulness. Or, because the revelation to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should challenge them with it before it occurred is evidence that he was sent by God, since the Messenger (ﷺ) had no means of knowing the times of the apparent changes of the celestial bodies. In light of this view, the restriction of its occurrence to Mecca rather than elsewhere in the world becomes clear. According to the first view, it was not noticed by anyone on earth except the people of Mecca, because they were not prepared for it, since it occurred at night, a time of heedlessness or sleep, and because the moon's appearance is not at one fixed moment for the people of the earth, for the times of its rising differ according to the regions, in the hours of night and day and in its passage over the sky.

Ibn Kaysan said: It is by way of anticipation and postponement (taqdim wa ta'khir). Its meaning: the moon split and the Hour drew near, because the original order in reporting events is to follow their order of occurrence, although the conjunction by "wa" (and) does not necessarily require order in occurrence.

Infashsha (انشق) is the reflexive form (mutawa') of shaqqahu, and the shaqq (split) is an opening and separation within the surface of a body such that a piece of the whole body does not separate from the rest. It is also called tasaddu' (cracking), as happens in a stick or a wall.

Thus, applying infishaq (splitting) to the occurrence of a crevice on the surface of the moon is a literal use. Applying it to the obscuring of part of its light is a metaphor (isti'ara). Applying it to its separation into two halves is a metonymy (majaz mursal).

Iqtiraab (اقتراب) originally has the form of reflexive derivation, meaning accepting the action of the agent, and here it is for emphasis of nearness. If it is taken in its literal sense of nearness, then it is a relative nearness, that is, the nearness of the Hour's arrival in the time yet to come, a nearness relative to what has passed of time from the creation of the heavens and the earth, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two," and he pointed with his index and middle fingers. For determining the duration from the time of the creation of the world, or from the time of the creation of man, is something people have no means of knowing. What is found in the books of the Jews is based on conjecture and imagination. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Every figure given for the age of this world is weak and frail. End quote.

The benefit of this consideration is that people turn to abandon polytheism, to multiply righteous deeds and avoid sins, because the Day of recompense is near.

As-Sa'a (the Hour) is a proper name by predominance for the time of the annihilation of this world. It is possible that by the Hour is meant a known hour about which they were warned in many verses, namely the hour of the uprooting of the polytheists by the swords of the Muslims.

If nearness is taken figuratively, meaning indication of possibility, then the meaning is: what people used to think impossible, the annihilation of the world, has become clear, since the occurrence of similar examples and parallels is persuasive of the possibility of even stronger examples.

The conjunction ﴿and the moon has split﴾ is a conjunction of one sentence to another.

The statement is used in a implied meaning (lazim ma'nahu), which is admonition, if the verse was revealed after the splitting of the moon as has been mentioned, because their knowledge of that is already established, so they have no need to be informed of the judgment of this report. Rather, they need reminder that among the signs of the approach of the Hour is that an eclipse occurs in the moon, which is what their admonition has repeatedly mentioned, as in His words, ﴿So when the sight is dazzled and the moon is eclipsed﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:7-8]. For what assures them that the splitting of the moon that occurred is not a sign of the nearness of the Hour? The splitting is only a type of eclipse, since the signs and marks of the Hour do not have fixed times in terms of nearness or distance from what they signal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 2:

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "This is continuous magic."﴾ It is possible that this is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to the report of the splitting of the moon, so that the word "sign" (ayah) in His words ﴿And if they see a sign﴾ refers to the moon. Indeed, it has come in some reports that when the polytheists saw the splitting of the moon, they said, "This is the magic of Muhammad ibn Abi Kabsha," and in another narration they said, "Muhammad has bewitched the moon." It is also possible that it is a new sentence (kalam mustani'af) within the description of their denial and obstinacy. On both interpretations, the occurrence of "sign" in an indefinite form (nakirah) within the context of a conditional clause (shart) conveys generality.

This report has been expressed in the form of a conditional to indicate that this is their habit and their constant practice.

The pronoun in "yarawa" (they see) refers to a pronoun not mentioned in the speech but indicated by the context, namely the polytheists, as occurs in many places in the Qur'an. Moreover, the story of the splitting of the moon and their criticism of it was well known at that time, and its witnesses were known. Thus they persist in it whenever they see a sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ.

The description "mustamirr" (continuous) may be derived from the verb marra, which is used metaphorically for passing away, with the sin and ta' serving to intensify the verb; that is, the moon does not remain split. It may also be derived from mirrah (with a kasra on the mim), meaning strength, with the sin and ta' indicating seeking; that is, a seeking of its action once, meaning strength, meaning its establishment (tamakkununa). The meaning is: this is a known, recurring magic, that is, such a thing is customary from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 3:

﴿Yet they denied and followed their own desires.﴾ This is an informing about their state in the past, after He had informed about their state in the future by the conditional in His saying ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾ [al-Qamar: 2]. The contrasting of that with this carries a kind of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which elements are omitted from each part and each part supplies what is missing from the other), as if it were said: "And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, 'Magic,' and they have already seen the signs and turned away and said, 'A continuous magic,' and they denied and followed their desires, and they will deny and follow their desires."

The conjunction of ﴿and followed their desires﴾ is the conjunction of cause to effect, because there is no impetus for their denial except following what their souls desire, namely the continuation of their state upon what they were accustomed to and knew, and whose lasting was well known.

He used the plural "desires" (ahwa larger) rather than saying "and followed the desire" as in His saying ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾ [al-An'am: 116], since hawa (desire) is a noun of genus that applies to the one and the many. He turned from the singular to the plural to match the plural pronoun attached to it, and to indicate that they have many kinds of desires: love of leadership, envy of the believers for what Allah has given them, love of following the religion of their fathers, love of their idols, attachment to their customs, and protectiveness of their pride.
* * *
﴿And every matter is settled.﴾
This is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the preceding speech, from His saying ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾ [al-Qamar: 2] up to His saying "their desires." It is thus an interpolation between the clause "and they denied" and the clause "and there had certainly come to them of the news," and the waw is interpolative. It runs in the manner of a proverb.

"Kull" (every) is among the nouns of generality. "Amr" (matter) is a noun denoting a high genus; similar to it are shay' (thing), mawjud (existent), and ka'in (being). It is specified by a qualifier, as in His saying ﴿When there comes to them a matter concerning security or fear, they spread it around﴾ [al-Nisa': 83], and it may be specified by reason or custom, just as shay' is specified in His saying about the wind of 'Ad: ﴿destroying everything﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25], meaning of the things capable of being destroyed. Here it generalizes to matters possessing influence, meaning that the effects of their realities are realized and their properties appear, even if obstacles intervene that prevent the attainment of their effects for a while, such as impediments preventing the appearance of their properties, or counteractions intended to remove their results, for influences do not fail to prevail over those obstacles and counteractions at the opportunities when they are able to manifest their effects and properties.

The statement is a metaphor (tamthil): the state of the effects of a reality oscillating between appearance and concealment until the time of their being able to manifest is likened to the state of a traveler going toward the desired place along various routes, near and far, until he settles in the desired place. It is an implicit (makniyya) metaphorical image, because the construction indicating the likened state was omitted and was alluded to by mentioning something of its concomitants, namely the description "settled" (mustaqirr).

Among this meaning is His saying ﴿For every news there is a settled time, and you will come to know﴾ [al-An'am: 67], which al-Kumayt ibn Zayd took up in his saying:

So now I have come to Umayya, and matters go to their destinations.

The "settling" meant in His saying "mustaqirr" is settling in this world.

In this there is an allusion, by implication, that the matter of the call of Muhammad ﷺ will take root and become settled after its turbulence.

Mustaqirr, with a kasra on the qaf, is an active participle of istaqarra, meaning qarra (to settle); the sin and ta' are for intensification, like the sin and ta' in istajaba.

The majority read the ra' of mustaqirr with a damma. Abu Ja'far read it with a kasra, making "kull amrin" a conjunction with "al-sa'a" (the Hour), with the sense: "and every matter has drawn near," and making "mustaqirr" an adjective of amr.

The meaning: their turning away from the signs, their slander against them by calling them magic or the like, and their denial of the truthful one and their collusion in that do not weaken the impact of these in souls, nor do they prevent their fruition. The matter of the Prophet ﷺ is heading toward the destiny of its true counterparts, of victory, completion, people's conviction in it, and the increase of its followers; and their following of their desires and their fabrication of excuses is heading toward the destiny of its false counterparts, of abandonment, exposure, and the diminishing of followers.

This appendage, in its generality, includes consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, a threat to the polytheists, and a call to the attention of the wavering.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verses 4–5:

﴿And there had certainly come to them of the news that which contains a deterrent﴾ ﴿—wisdom far-reaching—but warnings avail not.﴾ It is coordinated with the clause ﴿And they denied and followed their desires﴾ [al-Qamar: 3]. That is: there had come to them in the Qur'an, of the news of the nations, that which contains a deterrent for these people. Or, "the news" may be understood as the proofs (hujaj) contained in the Qur'an, meaning: there had come to them what is stronger in proof than the splitting of the moon. And ﴿of the news﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of "that which contains a deterrent," placed before what it explains, and min is explicative (bayaniyyah).

Al-muzdajar (the deterrent) is a mimi noun (a noun of place/instance formed from the root with a mim prefix), and it is formed in the pattern of the passive participle whose verb has more than three root letters. Izdajarahu means zajarahu (he restrained him), and the infixed ta' of the iftiʿal form here conveys intensification (lil-mubalaghah). The dal is a substitution for the ta' of the iftiʿal, which is replaced after the zay except in forms like izdada. That is: there is in it something that prevents them from committing what they committed. The meaning is: it is a restrainer for them. He made the deterrence (al-izdijar) figuratively "contained within" it, to intensify its constant presence with it, in the manner of abstraction (al-tajrid), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly in the Messenger of God you have a good example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], meaning: he is an example.

﴿Wisdom far-reaching﴾ is a substitute (badal) for (ma), meaning: there had come to them far-reaching wisdom.

Al-hikmah (wisdom) is perfection of understanding and soundness of intellect. What is meant here is speech that contains wisdom and conveys wisdom to its hearer, so describing speech as "wise" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), very common in usage, and it was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

Al-balighah (far-reaching) means reaching its target: it reaches the intended aim and benefits its possessor.

He then built upon it His saying ﴿but warnings avail not﴾, meaning: there had come to them that which contains a deterrent, yet that did not avail, that is, there did not occur in them a desisting from their misguidance.

(Ma) may be negative, meaning: the warnings do not avail them after that. This is a preparation for His saying ﴿So turn away from them﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. The present tense (al-mudari') covers both the present and the future, meaning: they are not beneficial. It implies by inference (bil-fahwa) that those news did not avail them in the past either, by a fortiori reasoning, for if what came to them of news does not avail them in restraint at present or in the future, then it did not avail them in the past; for had it availed them, the blame would have been lifted from them.

It is also possible that (ma) is interrogative for denunciation, meaning: what do warnings benefit among such stubborn, persistent people? That is, there is no benefit for them in those news. On this reading, (ma) is in the accusative position as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of tughni, and the noun it is annexed to has been omitted. The estimated meaning: "What kind of benefit do the warnings bring, when He is the one who informs of what distresses? For the news contains the sending of messengers from God as warners to their peoples. Yet they did not benefit them, and they did not profit from them." And because the news contains exhortation and warning against the like of their conduct, so it would be.

Thus the "warnings" (al-nudhur) means the verses of the Qur'an; each verse is treated as a warner, and it was pluralized as nudhur. It is also possible that it is the plural of nadhir in the sense of warning (al-indhar), as a verbal noun (ism masdar). This was discussed earlier, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56], at the end of Surat al-Najm.

**﴿So turn away from them﴾** is a consequence of **﴿so what good will warnings do﴾** [al-Qamar 54:5]. That is, turn away from disputing with them, for warnings do not benefit them. This is like His saying **﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance﴾** [al-Najm 53:29], meaning: you have delivered the message, so you are not responsible for their acceptance. This is what the Exalted said: **﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed﴾** [al-Dhariyat 51:54]. This is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and an assurance to him that he did not fall short in conveying the message. This verse has no bearing on the rulings of fighting them, since the context does not concern that, and its causes had not arisen at that time. So there is no basis for saying that it is abrogated (naskh).

**﴿On the Day when the Caller calls to a terrible thing﴾ ﴿with humbled eyes, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ ﴿hastening toward the Caller. The disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day."﴾** This is an explanatory resumption (istiʼnāf bayānī), because the command to turn away implies anger and a threat, and such a threat naturally prompts the listener to ask about the general nature of this threat. The purpose, therefore, is to censure them for not being deterred by what had come to them of these reports, by enumerating some of the important elements of those reports.

Do you not see that in that verse He mentioned His saying "before you," which is similar to what is here, along with the implicit indication that these people are turning away?

Know that it is said "kadhdhaba" (he denied) when someone says a statement that indicates denial, and it is also said "kadhdhaba" when someone believes that another is lying. God says: ﴿For they do not deny you﴾ [al-An'am: 33], in the reading of the majority with the doubling of the dhal. Both meanings are possible here. If the verb "kadhdhabat" is used here in the sense of saying denial, then the people of Noah confronted Noah directly by calling him a liar. If it is used in the sense of their belief in his lying, then their turning away from his warning and their neglect of joining him when he warned them of the flood indicates their belief.

The phrase "the people of Noah" is defined by its annexation to his name, since the nation in the time of Noah had no name by which they were known.

The denial is attributed to the whole people, because those who affirmed him were a small number. Indeed, only a few believed in him, as was mentioned earlier in Surah Hud.

Page 186
﴿And We left it as a sign, so is there anyone who will be mindful?﴾ The feminine pronoun refers back to ﴿the one carried on planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar: 13], meaning the ship. "Leaving" (al-tark) is a metaphor for preserving it and not removing it. Allah the Exalted says ﴿And We left in it a sign﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 37] in Surat al-Dhariyat, and He says ﴿And He left them in darkness, not seeing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] in Surat al-Baqarah, meaning: We preserved the ship of Nuh, safe from decay, so that it would be a sign witnessed by the nations to whom the messengers were sent, whenever one of the people near its place wished to see it. It serves as support for the messengers and as a warning through the first punishment with which a nation was punished after it denied its messenger, so it became a lasting proof, like the dwellings of Thamud.

Then it began to diminish until only some pieces of wood remained, which were witnessed by the earliest part of the Islamic nation, and it did not vanish until people from all nations after Nuh saw it. Thus the report of it became widely transmitted through direct observation, in support of the widely transmitted account of the Flood. The Qur'an has mentioned that it came to rest on Mount al-Judi, and from there Nuh and those with him descended, and the ship remained there, untouched by anyone, and this is among the reasons for its preservation from decay. The report is widely known that al-Judi is a small mountain near a village called Baqirda (with a kasra on the qaf, a sukun on the ra, and a fathah on the dal, shortened), from the island of Ibn 'Umar near Mosul, to the east of the Tigris.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Qatadah said: "The earliest part of this nation witnessed it." Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Ankabut ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 15], and this has been explained in detail there earlier.

The "aya" (sign) means a proof. The root meaning of aya is a distinguishing mark agreed upon by two or more persons: ﴿He said: My Lord, appoint for me a sign. He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 41].

Here He said ﴿And We left it﴾, while in Surat al-Ankabut He said ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 15], because its mention in Surat al-Qamar comes after the description of how it was built, the occurrence of the Flood, and Nuh's carrying [of the believers] in the ship. So He informs that it was kept after those circumstances, and the sign lies in its survival. In Surat al-Ankabut, the ship is mentioned from the outset, so He informs that Allah made it a sign when He revealed to Nuh how to build it, and the sign lies in its existence, which is what is expressed by ﴿We made it﴾.

From the preservation of the ship he derives the interrogative ﴿so is there anyone who will be mindful?﴾, asking who will remember through this sign, and this interrogative is used in the sense of urging remembrance of this sign and seeking out its report, like the interrogative in the words of Tarafah: "When the people say: who is the young man..." (the verse continues), and the urging is directed at everyone who receives these verses. The particle "min" is added to indicate the generality of the category in affirmative contexts, according to the more correct of the two opinions.

Mudakkir is originally mudhtakir, a form of the verb (ifti'al) from the dhikr (remembrance) with a damma on the dhal, meaning reflecting upon the evidence. The taa' of the iftial was changed into a dal because the two articulation points are close, and the dhal was assimilated into the dal for this reason. The recitation of this verse is specifically transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was mentioned earlier in Surat Yusuf: ﴿And he remembered after a period﴾ [Yusuf: 45].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 16:

﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾

This is a consequence drawn from the narrative, by what it contains in His words ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring forth﴾ [al-Qamar: 11] and so on to the end. "Kayfa" (how) is an interrogative about the state of the punishment, which is the punishment of the people of Nuh (Noah) by the flood. The interrogative is used to express wonder at the severity of this described punishment. The sentence serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil), and it contains an indirect warning (ta'ridh) to the polytheists that a punishment may befall them as a requital for their denying the Messenger (ﷺ), turning away from him, and harming him, just as it befell the people of Nuh.

The ya' of the first person (ya' al-mutakallim) has been omitted from "nudhur," and its original form is "nudhurî." Omitting it in speech when pausing is eloquent (fasih), and it occurs frequently in the Qur'an at the ends of verses (fawasil).

"Nudhur" is the plural of "nadhir" (warner), which is a verbal noun (ism masdar) of "andhara" (to warn), like "nidharah." It has been mentioned earlier in this surah. It is pluralized because the warning from the Messenger to his people was repeated, seeking their faith.

[Page 188]

When this warning was delivered through the Qur'an, while the polytheists turned away from listening to it and deprived themselves of its benefits, its report was followed by praise of the Qur'an's status, that it is from God and that God made it easy

and facilitated it so that people could be reminded by what they need of admonition, which is guidance and direction. This facilitation indicates God's care for it, like His saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. It is an insight for the Muslims, so that they increase in eagerness to study it, and an allusion to the polytheists, in the hope that they might desist from their aversion to it, as His saying ﴿So is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15] indicates.

The emphasis of the report with the lam and the particle of confirmation takes into account the state of the polytheists who doubted that it is from God.

Tayssir (facilitation): bringing about ease in something, either through an action, like His saying ﴿God intends ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], or through speech, like His saying ﴿We have made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember﴾ [al-Dukhan: 58].

Yusr (ease): simplicity and the absence of hardship in attaining what is sought from something. Since the Qur'an is speech, its facilitation returns to facilitating what is intended by speech, which is the listener's understanding of the meanings the speaker meant, without hardship for the listener and without constraint, as they say: "It enters the ear without permission." This ease arises from both the side of the words and the side of the meanings. As for the side of the words, it is through their being at the highest degree of eloquence of individual words and of structures, that is, the eloquence of speech, and the coherence of its whole, such that it is easy to retain on the tongues.

As for the side of the meanings, it is through the clarity of extracting them from the structures, and the abundance of the purposes the structures contain that are intended by them, and through meanings generating further meanings each time the contemplator reflects on understanding them.

The means of this cannot be encompassed by description, and its exposition has already preceded in the tenth introduction of this tafsir (exegesis). Among the most important of them is the conciseness of wording so that it quickly attaches to memory, and the generality of indications so that the minds of listeners may go in extracting meanings from them in every direction that the wording, the purpose and the context allow. Among them is also elaboration through explanation when the meanings contain some subtlety and obscurity.

This is achieved by composing the Qur'anic arrangement in a language that is the most eloquent of human languages, with the most permissive words and structures, abundant in meanings, and with its structures being the furthest that this language permits. So it is the choicest of the choice of the choice. God said: ﴿in clear Arabic speech﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195].

Then its recipients will be a community that is the most intelligent of nations in reason, the swiftest of them in understanding, the strongest of them in awareness of what they hear, and the longest of them in remembering it, without forgetting. Although they differ in these qualities, a difference that the law of creation requires, this difference in their condition does not contradict what God intended of facilitating the Reminder, because remembrance is a genus of the genera predicated by gradation (tashkik). However, when people of understanding gather to study and reflect upon it, meanings appear to their collectivity that none of them could enumerate alone.

God has imposed upon the scholars of the Qur'an the duty of explaining it, explicitly, as in His saying ﴿so that you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44], and implicitly, as in His saying ﴿And when God took the covenant of those given the Book: "You shall make it clear to the people"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187]. Indeed, this community is more worthy of this covenant.

In a hadith: "No people gather in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, except that tranquility descends upon them, mercy envelops them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him."

The lam in His saying "for the Reminder" is connected to "We have made easy," and it is an adverbial complement that is not fixed (ẓarf laghw ghayr mustaqirr). It is a lam that indicates that the action was done for the benefit of what the lam governs. So what the lam governs is not meant merely as the cause of the doer's action, as is the meaning of simple causation and the meaning of the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) in the accusative by the implied simple lam of causation. Rather, what is meant is that what this lam governs is a specific cause taken into account in bringing about the doer's action for its benefit. Thus what this lam governs cannot be the object (maf'ul), because the object of purpose is a cause in the more general sense, whereas what this lam governs is a specific cause. The object of purpose is like the cause of the action, and it is like what the ba' of causality governs, as in His saying ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40]. The genitive governed by this lam is like the genitive governed by the ba' of accompaniment, as in His saying ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. It also closely resembles the first object in the pattern of kasa (clothe) and a'ta (give). So this lam belongs to the category that Ibn Hisham, in Mughni al-Labib, called "quasi-possession" (shibh al-tamlik), and he followed Ibn Malik in Sharh al-Tashil in this.

Better than that is Ibn Malik's naming of it, in his commentary on his Kafiya and in al-Khulasa, as "transitivity" (ta'diyah). He was correct in this, because what the lam governs is what the verb to which the lam is attached has transitively reached, in the manner of the transitivity of a verb to its object. Ibn Hisham overlooked this precision. This is the fifth meaning of the prepositional lam in Mughni al-Labib, and he illustrated it with God's saying ﴿He made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. Ibn Malik, in Sharh al-Tashil, illustrated it with His saying ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ [Maryam: 5]. Among the examples suitable for it is His saying ﴿We made them subservient to them; of them some are for riding, and of them they eat﴾ [Ya Sin: 72], and His saying ﴿And We will make it easy for you toward ease﴾ [al-A'la: 8], and His saying ﴿So We will make it easy for him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl: 7], and His saying ﴿So We will make it easy for him toward hardship﴾ [al-Layl: 10]. Do you not see that what the lam governs in these examples indicates those who benefit from the objects of their verbs, so they are like the first of the two objects in the pattern of kasa?

We have expanded on this lam only because of the subtlety of its meaning, and so that the meaning of His saying ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ may become clear.

The primary meaning of the lam of genitive is causation, and from the use of the lam in figurative causation there arise meanings that became common and equal to the literal meaning. The grammarians made these into independent meanings for the sake of clarification.

Dhikr (remembrance): the verbal noun of dhakara, which is mental recollection, not verbal mention. The word dhikr with a dammah on the dhal, which is synonymous with it, is the name of the verbal noun. Dhikr is the recollection of what in its recollection there is benefit and averting of harm, and it is admonition and taking heed.

So the meaning of ﴿We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ becomes: the Qur'an's indication was made easy for the sake of the benefit of remembrance through that facilitation, so the swiftness of the arrangement of recollection upon hearing the Qur'an is made as a benefit for remembrance, because remembrance spreads and circulates through it, just as one who seeks something benefits when the means of attaining it are made easy for him and its distances are brought near to him. Thus in His saying ﴿We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ there is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), and the word "We have made easy" is an imaginative element (takhyil). The meaning reverts to: We have made the Qur'an easy for those who remember.

From this meaning He derived His saying ﴿So is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15]. What is said about it is like what was said about its counterpart mentioned just before, except that there is a subtle difference between the two kinds of remembrance. The earlier remembrance was remembrance of taking heed through observing the traces of the destroyed nations, whereas the remembrance here is remembrance upon hearing the Qur'an's compelling admonitions, understanding its meanings, and being guided by it.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 54 (al-Qamar), verses 18–20:

﴿The people of ʿĀd denied, so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind on a day of ill omen, continuing.﴾ ﴿It uprooted people as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees.﴾

The position of this sentence is like the position of the sentence ﴿Before them, the people of Noah denied﴾ (al-Qamar: 9). The apparent expectation was that it would be joined to it by a conjunction, but it was separated from it so that the speech would contain a repetition of rebuke, threat and lamentation over them, following His saying ﴿And there had certainly come to them of the news that which contained a deterrent﴾ (al-Qamar: 4) ﴿perfect wisdom, but warnings did not avail﴾ (al-Qamar: 5). The situation of rebuke and lamentation requires repetition.

The judgment that ʿĀd denied is a customary generality (ʿumūm ʿurfī), based on the fact that most of them denied him and only a small group believed in him. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us﴾ (Hud: 58).

He placed upon the reminder of ʿĀd's denial His saying ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ (al-Qamar: 16), before mentioning in the speech anything that indicates that God punished them, let alone a description of their punishment.

So the interrogative is used to arouse eagerness (tashwiq) for the report that follows it, and this is a metonymy (majaz mursal), because the interrogative entails a request for an answer, and the answer depends on the description of the punishment, which has not yet been mentioned, so that longing to know it arises. It is also an allusion (kināya) to the terrifying nature of that punishment.

In this interrogative there is a general indication of the state of the punishment, and this generality increases the eagerness for what follows it, namely His saying ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ and so on. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ (al-Naba: 1), then His saying ﴿about the great news﴾ (al-Naba: 2) and so on.

He conjoined (*wa nudhur*) to "My punishment" by supposing an elided genitive construction (muḍāf) indicated by the context. The implied meaning is: "and the consequence of My warnings," i.e., My warnings to them, that is, how the fulfilment of the threat that He warned them of came about.

"Nudhur" is the plural of *nadhīr* in the verbal-noun sense (bi'l-maʿnā al-maṣdarī), as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah. You have known from what we mentioned that the sentence ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ (al-Qamar: 16) here is not a repetition of its similar sentence in the account of the people of Noah, nor of the later one at the end of the story of ʿĀd, because of the difference that you have known between its meaning and the meaning of its counterpart, even though their wording is identical.

The eloquent speaker perceives the difference between them, and so he turns it away from the suspicion that this is a repetition. Since the description of the punishment of ʿĀd had not preceded, it was not appropriate for His saying ﴿so how was My punishment﴾ (al-Qamar: 16) to be an expression of wonder at the state of their punishment.

His saying "and warnings" is an admonition arising from the actualisation of God's threat against them. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) pointed to this, and we have followed it with an expansion and explanation. The question about the repetition of this sentence in the course of the story of ʿĀd here is raised by me in the book *Durrat al-Tanzil wa Ghurrat al-Ta'wil*, which is attributed to al-Fakhr and to al-Raghib, except that al-Fakhr's words in *al-Tafsir* are more worthy of reliance than what is in *Durrat al-Tanzil*.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ and so on is an explanation of the generality in His saying ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ (al-Qamar: 16). It takes the form of an answer to a formal interrogative. Both sentences convey an allusive threat to the polytheists of punishment for their denial.

The explanatory sentence describes the state of the punishment and not the state of the warning or the state of their messenger. This is sufficient, because denial implies the coming of a warner to them. And in the omitted object of "they denied" (*kadhdhabat*) there is an indication of their messenger, whom they denied. The sending of the messenger and their denial of him imply the warning, because when they denied him, his warning them became necessary.

The attribution of the sending of the wind to their pronoun is like the attribution of denial to them, on the basis of the general case, although God saved Hud and those with him, as you have known a moment ago. Or it refers back to the deniers, by the indication of His saying ﴿The people of ʿĀd denied﴾.

*Ṣarṣar*: the strong, powerful wind that has a sound. It was mentioned in Surah Fussilat.

By ﴿a day of ill omen﴾ is meant the first of the days of the wind that was sent upon ʿĀd, since it lasted seven days less one day, as in His saying ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of ill omen﴾ (Fussilat: 16) in Surah Fussilat, and His saying ﴿which He imposed upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ (al-Haqqah: 7) in Surah al-Haqqah.

*Naḥs*: bad condition.

The construct of "day" to "ill omen" (*naḥs*) is an idafa of time to what occurs in it, like the expressions "the day of shaving the forelock" and "the day of the conquest of Mecca." The day is attributed to ill omen only in terms of the one who is afflicted by it. So it is a day of ill omen for those who were punished, and a day of victory for the believers. The calamities of one people are gains for another people. There is no day among the days that is described as ill-omened or as fortunate, because every day brings ill fortune to some people and good fortune to others. What is narrated in reports concerning the specification of certain days of the year as inauspicious is among the errors of the storytellers, so a Muslim should not lend his ear to it.

It is well known among many Muslims to regard Wednesday as unlucky. The origin of this was carried over to them from the beliefs of the Magians of Persia. They call the Wednesday that falls at the end of the month "the Wednesday that does not return" (*al-arbiʿāʾ allatī lā tadūr*), meaning it does not recur. By this description they intended to specify the meaning of its being the last of the month, lest it be thought that the whole of the final half of the month is meant. Otherwise, what is the connection between not returning and misfortune? Every day of the week falls within the last week of the month and does not recur in that month.

From the poetry of one of the later (muwallad) poets of Khurasan:

*Your meeting with the early riser is an omen of ill, and your face is a Wednesday that does not return.*

Consult what was mentioned in Surah Fussilat.

*Mustamirr*: an adjective of *naḥs*, meaning a constant ill omen upon them. From the continuance is understood that it destroyed them, for if they had been saved, the ill omen would not have been continuous. *Mustamirr* is not an adjective of "day," since describing a day as continuous has no meaning.

The discussion of the derivation of *mustamirr* was mentioned a moment ago at His saying ﴿and they say, "Continuous magic"﴾ (al-Qamar: 2).

It may be derived from *marra al-shayʾu* used intransitively, when a thing is bitter (*murr*), and bitterness is metaphorically used for aversion and repugnance. Then it is a descriptive adjective (waṣf kāshif), because ill omen is detested.

*Nazʿ*: removal with force, so that no connection remains between the thing removed and what was connected to it. From it comes the expression "stripping off clothes."

*Aʿjāz*: the plural of *ʿajz*, which is the lowest part of a thing. The use of *ʿajz* for the last part of a thing became common, because they regard bodies as standing upright upon the earth, so the first part of them is what is toward the sky and the last part is what is next to the earth.

Here *aʿjāz* is applied to the roots of palm trees, because the root of the tree is at its last part, the part next to the earth.

The people lying prostrate on the earth are compared to the cut-off roots of palm trees that are uprooted from their places of growth because they have died, since their branches disappear and their leaves fall, so only the original trunks remain. For this reason they are called *aʿjāz*.

*Munqaʿir*: the active participle of *inqaʿara*, the intransitive form of *qaʿʿara*, meaning he reached its bottom by digging. One says "qaʿara the well" when he reached its depth. So the meaning is: as if they were trunks of palm trees whose insides had been hollowed out to their bottoms, which happens to the trunk of a palm when it has lain fallen for a long time.

*Munqaʿir* is a description of the palm trees. Its singular and masculine form was observed with respect to the form of the word *nakhl*, not to the number of what it denotes, in contrast to His saying ﴿as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ (al-Haqqah: 7) and His saying ﴿and palm trees with their sheaths﴾ (al-Rahman: 11).

Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: al-Mubarrad was asked in the presence of Isma'il al-Qadi about a thousand questions, among them: "What is the difference between His saying ﴿and for Solomon the wind, violent﴾ (al-Anbiya: 81), and ﴿there came to it a violent wind﴾ (Yunus: 22), and His saying ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ (al-Haqqah: 7) and ﴿trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾?" He said: "Everything that comes to you from this category, if you wish you may return it to the wording, using the masculine, or to the meaning, using the feminine." End of quotation.

The phrase ﴿as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the people." The reason for describing them as *munqaʿir* is an indication that the wind threw them down with such force that their bellies burst open, and their intestines and hearts were scattered, so they became empty corpses. This is a dreadful depiction of their state and a mutilation of them, to frighten whoever sees them.

The calamities of one people are gains for another people. There is no day among the days that is described as ill-omened or as fortunate, because every day brings ill fortune to some people and good fortune to others. What is narrated in reports concerning the specification of certain days of the year as inauspicious is among the errors of the storytellers, so a Muslim should not lend his ear to it.

It is well known among many Muslims to regard Wednesday as unlucky. The origin of this was carried over to them from the beliefs of the Magians of Persia. They call the Wednesday that falls at the end of the month "the Wednesday that does not return" (*al-arbiʿāʾ allatī lā tadūr*), meaning it does not recur. By this description they intended to specify the meaning of its being the last of the month, lest it be thought that the whole of the final half of the month is meant. Otherwise, what is the connection between not returning and misfortune? Every day of the week falls within the last week of the month and does not recur in that month.

From the poetry of one of the later (muwallad) poets of Khurasan:

*Your meeting with the early riser is an omen of ill, and your face is a Wednesday that does not return.*

Consult what was mentioned in Surah Fussilat.

He said: "Everything that comes to you from this category, if you wish you may return it to the wording, using the masculine, or to the meaning, using the feminine." End of quotation.

The reason for describing them as *munqaʿir* is an indication that the wind threw them down with such force that their bellies burst open, and their intestines and hearts were scattered, so they became empty corpses. This is a dreadful depiction of their state and a mutilation of them, to frighten whoever sees them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 54, verses 23–25:**

﴿Thamud denied the warnings.﴾ ﴿They said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us? Indeed, we would then be in error and madness."﴾ ﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us? Rather, he is a great liar, an arrogant one.﴾

The position of the clause ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ is like the position of the clause ﴿'Ad denied﴾ (Surah al-Qamar 54:18). Likewise, the attribution of the act of denial to Thamud, which is the name of a tribe, is commonly taken in the general sense, since Salih had been believed in by a small group, as God related about them in Surah al-A'raf.

*Thamud* is not declined (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) because of its status as a proper name (*'alamiyyah*) and its semantic feminine gender (*ta'nith ma'nawi*), that is, by interpreting the name as "the tribe."

*Al-nudhur* (النُّذُر) is the plural of *nadhir* (نَذِير), which is an ism al-masdar (verbal noun) of *andhara* (أنذر). That is, they denied the warnings (*al-indharat*) with which God warned them through His Messenger. *Al-nudhur* here cannot be taken as the plural of *nadhir* in the sense of "warner," because when the verb of denial is transitive to the person accused of lying, it takes its object directly without a preposition, as God says: ﴿So they denied My messengers﴾ (Surah Saba' 34:45), ﴿When they denied the messengers﴾ (Surah al-Furqan 25:37), and ﴿And if they deny you﴾ (Surah al-Hajj 22:42). When it is transitive to the statement that is denied, it takes *bi* (بِ), as God says: ﴿And you denied it﴾ (Surah al-An'am 6:57), ﴿Your people denied it﴾ (Surah al-An'am 6:66), and ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:40), and He says *kadhdhabu bi-ayatina*. This differs from His saying ﴿Thamud denied the messengers﴾ (Surah al-Shu'ara' 26:141) in Surah al-Shu'ara'.

The meaning is that they denied the warnings of their Messenger, that is, they rejected them, and then they denied their Messenger. For this reason, God placed after the clause ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ His saying ﴿They said: "Shall we follow a single human being..."﴾ up to His saying ﴿Rather, he is a great liar, an arrogant one.﴾ If the intended meaning of *al-nudhur* were the plural of *nadhir*, applied to their warner, the proper arrangement of the discourse would be for the clause ﴿They said: "Shall we follow a single human being..."﴾ and what follows to come without being joined by *fa* (فَ), because it would then be an explanation of the clause ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾.

The meaning is that Salih brought them the warnings, and they rejected them. Their doubt in denying was what their saying ﴿Shall we follow a single human being...﴾ to the end expresses. This statement therefore implies that it was a reply to a call and a warning. The reason that the denial of Thamud is detailed while the denial of 'Ad is summarized is to show the resemblance between their denial and the denial of the Quraysh, since their statements were similar.

Regarding the coherence of the clause ﴿They said: "Shall we follow a single human being..."﴾ and so on after the clause ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ (Surah al-Qamar 54:9): this is a statement they made to their Messenger when he warned them with the warnings, because His saying *kadhdhabat* (denied) on that day implies a reporter, since denial requires the existence of one who reports. It was a statement they addressed to Salih directly, and he is the one they meant by their saying ﴿a human being from among us﴾ and so on. They shifted from the second person address to the third person.

*Basharan* (أبَشَرًا) is in the accusative as the object of *nattabi'uhu* (نَتَّبِعُهُ) by the construction known as *al-ishtighal* (الاشتغال, the verbal-occupation construction, in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to a noun placed before it). It was placed first because it is attached to the interrogative hamza (هَمْزَةُ الاسْتِفْهام), whose proper place is at the beginning, and it is attached to it rather than the hamza entering on *nattabi'*, because the locus of the denying interrogative is the fact that a human being is followed, not that they follow him. Similar is ﴿Shall a human being guide us?﴾ (Surah al-Taghabun 64:6). This is among the subtleties of the positions of interrogative particles, as explained in the science of meanings ('ilm al-ma'ani).

The interrogation here is denying (*inkari*). They denied that God would send to people a human being like themselves; that is, if God had willed, He would have sent angels.

The description of *basharan* (بَشَرًا) by *wahidan* (واحِدًا) may carry one of the following meanings. First, that he was alone in his call, having neither followers nor helpers, that is, he was not one who is feared, in contrast to the saying of the people of Madyan: ﴿Were it not for your kinsmen, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us﴾ (Surah Hud 11:91). Second, that he was one of the ordinary individuals among them, that is, not one of our best. Third, that he was alone in claiming prophethood, having no predecessor in it, like the saying of Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi:

*"I was once the most self-sufficient of people, one person,*
*who lived in Medina, among the farmers of Fum."*

He means: no one contends with me in that.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we would then be in error and madness﴾ is a justification for their denial that they should follow a human being from among them. Its estimated sense is: "Shall we follow you, while you are a single human being from among us?"

*Idhan* (إذًا) is a particle of response, and it links the clause to the one before it. *Al-dalal* (الضَّلال, error) is the failure to find the way. They meant: we would then be mistaken in our affair.

*Al-su'ur* (السُّعُر) is madness. It is said with a *damma* on the *'ayn* or with it being sukun (silent).

Ibn 'Abbas explained *al-su'ur* as punishment, taking it as the plural of *sa'ir* (سَعِير, blaze). The clause ﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ is a justification for the denying interrogative.

*Ulqiya* (أُلْقِيَ) is literally: thrown from the hand to the ground. Here it is used metaphorically for the sending down of the Reminder from heaven, as God says: ﴿Indeed, We shall cast upon you a heavy word﴾ (Surah al-Muzzammil 73:5).

*Fi* (فِي) here is for metaphorical containment (*al-zarfiyyah al-majaziyyah*). They made their being clothed in error and madness like the being of a contained thing within a container.

*Min baynina* (مِن بَيْنِنا) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *'alayhi* (عَلَيْهِ), that is: how is the Reminder cast upon him rather than upon us? They meant that among them there is someone more deserving than he to be revealed to, according to the perceptions of the ignorant who measure the matter by the measures of the deficiency of their understanding, and who suppose that the causes of preference in customs are the same as its causes in realities.

The particle *min* (مِن) in *min baynina* carries the meaning of separation (*al-fasl*), as Ibn Malik named it, though Ibn Hisham rejected this. That is, separated from among us, as in God's saying: ﴿And God knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:220).

﴿Rather, he is a great liar, an arrogant one.﴾ is a turning away (*idrab*, a change of direction) from what they denied by their saying "Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?" That is: the Reminder has not been sent down upon him from among us, but rather he is a liar in what he claims, insolent and arrogant.

*Al-ashir* (الأشِر), with a *kasra* on the *shin* and a light *ra'*, is the active participle of *ashira*, which means to rejoice excessively and to be insolent. The meaning is: he is self-admiring, claiming what is not in him.

*Al-nudhur* (النُّذُر) is the plural of *nadhir* (نَذِير), which is an ism al-masdar (verbal noun) of *andhara* (أنذر). The meaning is that they denied the warnings of their Messenger, that is, they rejected them, and then they denied their Messenger. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 26:

﴿Soon they will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent one.﴾ It is a suppressed saying (maqul qawl mahdhuf), indicated by the context, and its estimated form is: "We said to their warner," which is indicated by His saying ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ [al-Qamar: 23]. For the warnings (al-nudhur) require a warner for them, and this is what fits His saying after it, ﴿So wait and be patient for them﴾ [al-Qamar: 27]. This is based on the premise that His saying just before, ﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human from among us?"﴾ [al-Qamar: 24], is a statement with which they answered the warning of Salih to them, the warning implied in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ [al-Qamar: 23]. With this the discourse is arranged in the most complete arrangement.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "sa-ya'lamun" with the ya' of the third person. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "sa-ta'lamun" (ستعلمون) with the ta' of address. This may be the relating of a speech from God to Salih, with the estimate: "We said to him: Say to them," so it contains an omitted saying. It may also be an address from God to them, with the estimate: "We said to them: you will know." It may also be an address to the polytheists, by making the sentence parenthetical (mu'taridah).

By "tomorrow" (ghadan) is meant the near future time, as in their proverb: "Indeed with today there is a tomorrow," i.e., indeed with the present time there is a future time. It is said to console oneself for the oppression of an oppressor or the like. al-Tirimmah said:

"And before tomorrow, woe to my heart from a tomorrow, when my companions depart, and I am not departing."

He means the day of his death. Its meaning in the verse is the day of the descent of their near punishment. Its clarification is in His saying ﴿Indeed We are sending the she-camel as a trial for them﴾ [al-Qamar: 27], etc., i.e., when they see the miracle and the flashes of punishment appear to them, they will know that they are the liars, the insolent ones, not Salih.

On the second reading regarding the pronoun in (sa-ya'lamun), "tomorrow" is meant as the day of the victory of the Muslims at Badr and the day of the conquest of Makkah, i.e., they will know from who is the liar, one resembling the liar in the story of Thamud.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verses 27–29:

﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel as a trial for them, so watch them and be patient.﴾ ﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them, each drink being attended.﴾ ﴿But they called their companion, and he took [the sword] and hamstrung [her].﴾

This sentence explains the sentence ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent one﴾ [al-Qamar: 26], with respect to what the explained sentence (with a fatha on the ya') contains of threat and of bringing near its time. In it is also confirmation of the Messenger whom they denied.

The pronoun in (lahum) ("for them") is in accordance with the apparent sense according to the reading of the majority, sayaʿlamūna with the ya' of the third-person feminine. As for the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah, (sa-taʿlamūna) with the ta' of address, the pronoun (lahum) is then an iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

The sending of the she-camel is a reference to the story of the miracle of Salih, that he brought forth for them a she-camel from a rock. That miracle was the preface to the causes for which punishment was hastened upon them, so he mentioned this story within the explanatory sentence as a preparation and a introduction.

The "sending" is a metaphor for making her a sign for Salih. The creation of extraordinary events to support the messengers has been known by the name of "sending" in the Qur'an, as the Exalted said ﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning﴾ [al-Isra': 59]. So the she-camel is likened to a witness whom Allah sent to support His messenger. This indicates that in this she-camel there is a miracle, and He named her a sign in His saying, relating from them and from Salih, ﴿So bring a sign, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 154] ﴿He said: this is a she-camel﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 155], etc.

(Fitnatan lahum) is a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddar), meaning: it tests them with a trial, which is their obstinacy in its indication of the truthfulness of their Messenger. The sense of the speech in estimation: Indeed, We are sending the she-camel as a sign for you and a trial for them.

The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the deniers among them, by the indication of the attribution of denial as previously mentioned. The active participle in ﴿mursilu al-naqah﴾ is used in the future by way of metaphor, by the indication of His saying ﴿so watch them and be patient﴾; so it departs from saying "sanursilu" (we will send) to the real form of the active participle in the present, to bring the time of the future close to the time of the present.

Al-irtiqab is waiting; irtaqaba is like raqaba, and it is more eloquent in meaning than raqaba, due to the increase in its form.

The verb of irtiqab is transitive to their selves (damā'ir-hum) by the estimation of a genitive complement that the speech requires, because one does not wait for their essences, but waits for conditions that will occur to them. This is the manner of attributing or linking derivative nouns whose meanings are not attributed to essences, so it is by estimation of a genitive complement, a brevity in speech relying on the clarity of the meaning. Like the attribution of prohibition and permission to essences in His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The meaning: wait for what will befall them of trial at the appearance of the she-camel.

Al-istibar is strong patience, and it is likewise, like irtiqab, stronger in meaning than sabr: be patient with a patience that is not affected by weariness or distress, i.e., be patient over their denial and do not despair of victory over them. The complement of (required: ismbir) is omitted so that it covers every state that calls for distress. The estimation: and be patient over their harm and over what you find in yourself of awaiting victory.

The clause ﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾, by the consideration that the promise of creating the sign of the she-camel requires an omitted speech, its estimation: So We sent to them the she-camel and said: inform them that the water is to be shared between them, following the manner of conjunction and omission in His saying ﴿So We revealed to Musa: strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], even though the conjunctive particle differs. Such omission is frequent in the Qur'an's concision.

The definite article in (al-ma') ("the water") is for prior knowledge, i.e., the water of the town from which they draw, for each settlement that a people alights at has water for their watering. And He said ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23].

He informed about the water that it is a "division" (qismah). The meaning is "divided," so it is from the report by the verbal noun for emphasis and exaggeration.

The pronoun in (baynahum) refers to what is known from the context after mention of the water, since it is well-known that the people of the town draw from it for themselves and their livestock. When the she-camel was mentioned, it was known that she would not do without drinking, so the pronoun of the rational beings prevailed over the pronoun of the single she-camel. Since the she-camel had no particular owner, God ordained for her a turn at the water. In the verse in Surat al-Shu'ara' it came: ﴿He said: this is a she-camel; she has a drink, and you have the drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 155]. This is the origin of the trial, for it is related that on her drinking day the she-camel would drink all the water of the well, so they were stingy about that and concealed their hatred of her from the water. Then Salih informed them that Allah forbids them from touching her with harm.

The (muhtadar), with a fatha on the dad, is a passive participle from ihdar, which is the opposite of absence. The meaning: "present/attended," i.e., it is present for it, and the complement is omitted because of its presence. This is among what their Messenger was commanded to inform them of: that the people do not attend on the day of the she-camel's drink, and she, by Allah's inspiration, does not attend on the days of the people's drink. The shirb (drink), with a kasra on the shin, is the turn of drawing water.

Then they called their companion, the one whom they incited to kill her, and he is Qudar (with a damma on the qaf and a light dal), son of Salif. He was known among the Arabs as Ahmar (the Red). Zuhayr said:

*Then she will produce for you boys, all of them most ill-omened, like the Red One of 'Ad; then you will suckle and wean.*

He means the Red One of Thamud, since Thamud are brothers of 'Ad. I have not found the reason for describing him as Ahmar, and I suppose it is for the whiteness of his face. In the hadith: "I was sent to the red and the black." Qudar was one of their chiefs and men of might among them. The Prophet ﷺ likened him to Abu Zam'ah, meaning al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad, in his saying: a man of strength among his people was summoned, like Abu Zam'ah, i.e., he answered their call, struck her with an arrow and killed her.

He expressed "their companion" to indicate that they were content with his deed, since they accompanied him and colluded with him.

Their calling to him was a calling of incitement against the she-camel, and they called him only because he was known for boldness and little concern, owing to his might.

Ta'ata is the reflexive (mutawa'a) of 'ata, and it is derived from 'ata ya'tu, when one takes hold. The form tafa'ala requires a plurality of agents: the fear of the people about killing her, in response to what their Messenger had warned them of of the threat, and their hesitation to proceed to kill her by passing (the weapon) to one another, is likened to the act of handing over, so that each one, when he shrinks from directly doing it and points to another, is as if he hands what is in his hand to the hand of another, until Qudar took it.

He joined (fa-'aqara) with the fa' to indicate the swiftness of his carrying out what they had called him for.

Al-'aqr: its origin is striking a camel with a sword on its hamstrings so that it falls to the ground kneeling, so that the slaughterer may be able to slaughter it. Abu Talib said:

*Striking with the edge of the sword the shanks of her heaven, when they lack provision, indeed you are the hamstringer.*

Its use became general for killing a camel, as here, since the intended meaning is not that he hamstrung her but that he killed her with his arrow.
