(Fitnatan lahum) is a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddar), meaning: it tests them with a trial, which is their obstinacy in its indication of the truthfulness of their Messenger. The sense of the speech in estimation: Indeed, We are sending the she-camel as a sign for you and a trial for them.

The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the deniers among them, by the indication of the attribution of denial as previously mentioned. The active participle in ﴿mursilu al-naqah﴾ is used in the future by way of metaphor, by the indication of His saying ﴿so watch them and be patient﴾; so it departs from saying "sanursilu" (we will send) to the real form of the active participle in the present, to bring the time of the future close to the time of the present.

Al-irtiqab is waiting; irtaqaba is like raqaba, and it is more eloquent in meaning than raqaba, due to the increase in its form.

The verb of irtiqab is transitive to their selves (damā'ir-hum) by the estimation of a genitive complement that the speech requires, because one does not wait for their essences, but waits for conditions that will occur to them. This is the manner of attributing or linking derivative nouns whose meanings are not attributed to essences, so it is by estimation of a genitive complement, a brevity in speech relying on the clarity of the meaning. Like the attribution of prohibition and permission to essences in His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The meaning: wait for what will befall them of trial at the appearance of the she-camel.

Al-istibar is strong patience, and it is likewise, like irtiqab, stronger in meaning than sabr: be patient with a patience that is not affected by weariness or distress, i.e., be patient over their denial and do not despair of victory over them. The complement of (required: ismbir) is omitted so that it covers every state that calls for distress. The estimation: and be patient over their harm and over what you find in yourself of awaiting victory.

The clause ﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾, by the consideration that the promise of creating the sign of the she-camel requires an omitted speech, its estimation: So We sent to them the she-camel and said: inform them that the water is to be shared between them, following the manner of conjunction and omission in His saying ﴿So We revealed to Musa: strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], even though the conjunctive particle differs. Such omission is frequent in the Qur'an's concision.

The definite article in (al-ma') ("the water") is for prior knowledge, i.e., the water of the town from which they draw, for each settlement that a people alights at has water for their watering. And He said ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23].

He informed about the water that it is a "division" (qismah). The meaning is "divided," so it is from the report by the verbal noun for emphasis and exaggeration.

The pronoun in (baynahum) refers to what is known from the context after mention of the water, since it is well-known that the people of the town draw from it for themselves and their livestock. When the she-camel was mentioned, it was known that she would not do without drinking, so the pronoun of the rational beings prevailed over the pronoun of the single she-camel. Since the she-camel had no particular owner, God ordained for her a turn at the water. In the verse in Surat al-Shu'ara' it came: ﴿He said: this is a she-camel; she has a drink, and you have the drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 155]. This is the origin of the trial, for it is related that on her drinking day the she-camel would drink all the water of the well, so they were stingy about that and concealed their hatred of her from the water. Then Salih informed them that Allah forbids them from touching her with harm.

The (muhtadar), with a fatha on the dad, is a passive participle from ihdar, which is the opposite of absence. The meaning: "present/attended," i.e., it is present for it, and the complement is omitted because of its presence. This is among what their Messenger was commanded to inform them of: that the people do not attend on the day of the she-camel's drink, and she, by Allah's inspiration, does not attend on the days of the people's drink. The shirb (drink), with a kasra on the shin, is the turn of drawing water.

Then they called their companion, the one whom they incited to kill her, and he is Qudar (with a damma on the qaf and a light dal), son of Salif. He was known among the Arabs as Ahmar (the Red). Zuhayr said:

*Then she will produce for you boys, all of them most ill-omened, like the Red One of 'Ad; then you will suckle and wean.*

He means the Red One of Thamud, since Thamud are brothers of 'Ad. I have not found the reason for describing him as Ahmar, and I suppose it is for the whiteness of his face. In the hadith: "I was sent to the red and the black." Qudar was one of their chiefs and men of might among them. The Prophet ﷺ likened him to Abu Zam'ah, meaning al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad, in his saying: a man of strength among his people was summoned, like Abu Zam'ah, i.e., he answered their call, struck her with an arrow and killed her.

He expressed "their companion" to indicate that they were content with his deed, since they accompanied him and colluded with him.

Their calling to him was a calling of incitement against the she-camel, and they called him only because he was known for boldness and little concern, owing to his might.

Ta'ata is the reflexive (mutawa'a) of 'ata, and it is derived from 'ata ya'tu, when one takes hold. The form tafa'ala requires a plurality of agents: the fear of the people about killing her, in response to what their Messenger had warned them of of the threat, and their hesitation to proceed to kill her by passing (the weapon) to one another, is likened to the act of handing over, so that each one, when he shrinks from directly doing it and points to another, is as if he hands what is in his hand to the hand of another, until Qudar took it.

He joined (fa-'aqara) with the fa' to indicate the swiftness of his carrying out what they had called him for.

Al-'aqr: its origin is striking a camel with a sword on its hamstrings so that it falls to the ground kneeling, so that the slaughterer may be able to slaughter it. Abu Talib said:

*Striking with the edge of the sword the shanks of her heaven, when they lack provision, indeed you are the hamstringer.*

Its use became general for killing a camel, as here, since the intended meaning is not that he hamstrung her but that he killed her with his arrow.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 30:

﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾

The discussion of it is like the discussion of its counterpart occurring in the story of the people of Noah. It is not a repetition, but it is specific to this story.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 31:

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single blast, and they became like the crumbled remains of one who builds a stable-pen.﴾ This is the answer to His words ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ [al-Qamar: 30]. Its position is like that of His words ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ [al-Qamar: 19] in the story of 'Ad, as has already been explained.

The "ṣayḥah" (blast) is the thunderbolt (al-ṣā'iqah), which is referred to as "al-ṭāghiyah" in surah al-Haqqah and as "al-rajfah" (the quake) in surah al-A'raf. It is a great thunderbolt that broke the customary order, and it destroyed them. For this reason it is described as "single" (wāḥidah), to indicate that it was extraordinary and broke the customary order, since it struck an entire tribe, namely the people of al-Hijr (Ashab al-Hijr).

"Kānū" (they became) means "ṣārū" (they became), and "kāna" comes with the meaning of "ṣāra" when it is intended to express a specific, newly occurring state that did not exist before.

Page 203

"Al-hashīm" is what has dried out and withered of herbage and trees. It is derived from "al-hashm," which means breaking, because dry matter of this kind becomes quick to break. Here the term refers to a particular kind of it: the dried branches of thorny trees (al-'iḍah) and the thorns and large herbage that people used to make into enclosures (ḥaẓā'ir) to protect their flocks from the wind and from predators. For this reason "al-hashīm" is attributed to "al-muḥtazir." "Al-muḥtazir," with a kasra on the ẓā' (pointed letter), is the one who makes and builds the enclosure. He gathers the dry matter and lays it on the ground so that he can afterward arrange it as a fence for his enclosure. Thus the thing compared is the dry matter gathered on the ground before it is fenced. For this reason He said "like the crumbled remains of one who builds a stable-pen" and did not say "like the crumbled remains of the enclosure," because the intended point of comparison is its state before it is arranged and woven together, and before it is made into an enclosure.

"Al-muḥtazir" is of the form "mufta'il" derived from "ḥaẓīrah" (enclosure), meaning one who takes on the task of making an enclosure.

The discussion about the verb "arsalnā" taking "ʿalayhim" (upon them), with the pronoun referring to Thamud, is the same as the discussion regarding ﴿We sent upon them a furious wind﴾ [al-Qamar: 19].

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ This is a second repetition, following its two counterparts earlier in the accounts of the people of Noah and the people of 'Ad. It serves as a concluding refrain (tadhyil) for this narrative, just as the two earlier narratives were concluded with their counterparts. The context of favour (imtinan) and urging toward reflection (tadabbur) upon the Qur'an called for the repetition, because reflecting upon it leads to avoiding error and guides one to the paths of guidance. This is more important than the repetition of ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ [al-Qamar: 30], and therefore it was given precedence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verses 33–35:

﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a torrential wind, except the family of Lot; We saved them at dawn.﴾ ﴿As a favour from Us. Thus do We reward those who give thanks.﴾

The discussion of its individual words is like the discussion of their counterparts elsewhere, and the story of the people of Lot has already been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf and elsewhere.

Page 204

He identified the people of Lot by attributing them to him, since that nation had no name by which the Arabs knew them.

The response of the people of Lot to Lot's call is not related here, as it was related in the three stories before this one. It was related in Surat al-A'raf, in Surat Hud and in Surat al-Hijr, because Surat al-Qamar is built upon warning the polytheists about their turning away from taking heed of the signs of God that they had witnessed, and of the traces of His signs upon the earlier nations, whose reports they knew and whose traces they had seen. There was therefore no reason to detail the statements of those nations, except for what resembled the statements of the polytheists in their detail. The statements of the people of Lot were not of that standing, so it was limited, in their case, to relating what they shared with the polytheists, namely the denial of their messenger and their turning away from his warnings. The warnings have already been mentioned.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a torrential wind﴾ is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani) arising from the report that the people of Lot denied the warnings.

Likewise the sentence ﴿We saved them at dawn﴾, and the sentence ﴿Thus do We reward those who give thanks﴾.

Al-hasib (الحاصب) is the wind that pelts, i.e. it throws up pebbles, lifting them from the ground because of its strength. It has been mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Of them We sent upon some a torrential wind﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40] in Surat al-'Ankabut.

The exception is genuine, because the family of Lot are among his people.

The family (al in Al Lut) of Lot are his kin, namely his daughters, and Lot is included by way of implication (dalalat al-fahwa). It has been mentioned in other verses that Lot's wife was not saved by God, and this is not mentioned here, being sufficed by the places where it is mentioned, and as an alert that whoever does not believe in the messenger is not counted among his family, as He said ﴿O Noah, he is not of your family; his deed is unrighteous﴾ [Hud: 46].

Mention of "at dawn" (bisahar), i.e. at the time of the pre-dawn, is to indicate their deliverance shortly before the punishment descended upon their people, according to His words after it ﴿And certainly a lasting punishment came upon them early in the morning﴾ [al-Qamar: 38].

The word "favour" (ni'mah) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the speaker's pronoun, i.e. as a bounty from Us.

The sentence ﴿Thus do We reward those who give thanks﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah), and it is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani) relating to the sentence ﴿We saved them at dawn﴾, in view of the circumstantial phrase that accompanies it, i.e. as a bounty because he gave thanks. In this there is an intimation that the destruction of others was because they disbelieved, and this is an implicit warning to the polytheists and a glad tiding to the believers.

In His saying "from Us" (min 'indina) there is an emphasis on the significance of this bounty, because the adverbial "'inda" indicates storing up and exclusive possession, like "ladun" in His saying "from Us" (min ladunna). That is more eloquent than saying "a bounty from Us" or "We bestowed."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 36:

﴿And certainly He had warned them of Our assault, but they disputed the warnings.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a torrential wind﴾ [al-Qamar: 34].

The emphasis of the statement by the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) and the particle of certainty (harf al-tahqiq) is intended to stress the purpose for which the story was related, which is the admonition of the Quraysh, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had warned, so they disputed the warnings.

Al-batshah is a single instance of al-batsh, which is seizing with force for punishment or the like. It was discussed earlier, in His saying ﴿Or do they have hands with which they strike?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195], at the end of Surah al-A'raf. Here it is a figurative expression (tamthil) for swift destruction, like His saying ﴿The Day We will strike with the greatest striking﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16] in Surah al-Dukhan.

Al-tamari is a reciprocal form (tafaʿul) from al-miraʾ, which means doubt. The form of mufaʿalah here indicates intensification. The verb tamaraw has been given the implied sense of "they denied" (kaththabu), and so it takes the preposition bi-. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ [al-Najm: 55], in Surah al-Najm.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 37:**

﴿And they had already sought to turn him away from his guests, so We blinded their eyes, [saying], "Taste My punishment and My warnings."﴾ This is a summary of what is mentioned in other surahs about the story of the people of Lut (Lot): that a guest came to him, his people desired to commit indecency with them, Lut was unable to repel his people when they forced their way into his house, and Allah blinded their eyes so that they could not see how to enter.

[Page 206]

*Murawadah* (an attempt to win over someone who dislikes something by getting him to accept what he dislikes) is an *mufa'alah* (a verbal form expressing mutual or repeated action) from *rada yarudu rawdan*, meaning to go and return regarding a matter. The state of one who repeatedly returns to a request and attempts it is depicted by the state of one who departs and then returns. *Rawaduhu* is used here with the sense of *dafa'uhu* (they pushed him away) and *sarafuhu* (they turned him away), so it takes *'an* (from/away from).

The attribution of *murawadah* to the people of Lut is made by means of their pronoun, even though only a group of them were the ones who made the attempt, because what they sought from him was the rejection of all the people, regardless of who specifically carried it out.

The phrase ﴿'an dayfihi﴾ ("from his guests") is connected to the verb *rawadu*, with an elided noun understood, meaning: "from enabling them to have his guests."

His saying ﴿fa-dhuquu 'adhabi wa nudhur﴾ [al-Qamar: 39] is the object of an elided verb of speech, indicated by the context of the discourse, addressed to the group whose eyes We blinded: ﴿Taste My punishment﴾, which is blindness; that is, Allah placed in their souls that this was a punishment for them.

He used *al-dhawq* (tasting) for perceiving the punishment as a figurative usage (*majaz mursal*, a figure of speech in which the word is used for a related meaning) by the relationship of *taqyid* ("restriction", meaning the sense is restricted to perception).

He conjoined *al-nudhur* (warnings) to *al-'adhab* (punishment) on the basis that the punishment is a confirmation of the warnings; that is, "Taste the fulfilment of My warnings." The transitivity of the verb *dhuquu* to *nudhuri* is through an elided noun, meaning "and the consequences of My warnings."

The discussion of its emphasis with the particle of oath (*lam al-qasam*) has already been covered, and the *ya'* of the first person was dropped from *nudhuri* for lightness.

Surah 54, verse 38: "And certainly the punishment settled upon them at dawn."

The discussion of its emphasis with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) has already been covered in its counterpart above.

Al-bukrah (البُكْرَةُ) means the first part of the day, which is the time of dawn. In the other verse Allah says: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?﴾ [Hud: 81]. He mentioned "bukrah" to indicate the hastening of the punishment upon them.

At-tasbih (التَّصْبِيحُ) means being present at the time of morning, which is the first part of the day.

Al-mustaqirr (المُسْتَقِرُّ) means that which is firm and lasting, proceeding with one constant force, not ceasing until it uprooted them completely.

Al-'adhab (العَذابُ, the punishment) is the sinking of the earth (al-khasf) and the rain of stones, and it is mentioned in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud.

Qur'an 54:39: ﴿So taste My punishment and My warnings.﴾ This is a continuation (tafri') of a statement that has been omitted, addressed to them, and intended as a rebuke (tawbikh). It may be that it was cast into their minds (ruw') at the arrival of the punishment, by God placing a sound in their ears.

The address is to all those who were struck by the established punishment, and for this reason this sentence is not a repetition. The ya' of the first person has been dropped from the word "nudhuri" for lightness.

The discussion of the usage of "dhawq" (tasting) here is like its usage in the preceding verse.

The benefit of informing them of what was said to them, "So taste My punishment and My warnings" [al-Qamar: 37], in both places, is that with the hearing of each report of this there is renewed for them remembrance (idkar), admonition (i'tiz) and awakening (iqaz), in fulfilment of the right of the Qur'anic reminder (tadhkir).

﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾

This is the third repetition, emphasizing the status of the Qur'an because of the distinctive quality mentioned in the passages where its counterpart and similar verses were repeated, especially in its immediately following counterpart, which is connected to it. Here he did not mention ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ [al-Qamar: 30], being content with narrating the punishment inflicted on the people of Lot, as an allusion that serves as a warning to the polytheists.

[Page 208]

﴿And the warners had certainly come to the family of Pharaoh. They denied Our signs, all of them, so We seized them with the seizure of One Mighty and Powerful.﴾

Since Musa's (peace be upon him) call was not directed to the Coptic nation, and its purpose was not to give them legislation, but it was directed to Pharaoh and the people of his state, who controlled the affairs of the Pharaonic kingdom, so that they would permit the Children of Israel to be released from enslavement and enable them to leave with Musa, he specifically mentioned here "the family of Pharaoh," meaning Pharaoh and his household, because the decision came from their opinion. Do you not see that Pharaoh did not single out the rejection of Musa's call for himself, but said to those around him: ﴿Will you not listen?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 25], and said ﴿What do you advise?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 35], and they said ﴿Delay him and his brother﴾ [al-A'raf: 111], and so on. This sentence serves as a conclusion to the summary of the stories about the nations that denied the messengers, from the people of Noah onward, and those who came after them. For this reason it is separated from what precedes it and not joined to it by a conjunction.

It shifts the style of speech from being addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ) to being addressed to the polytheists, in order to move from allusion to explicit statement, out of concern for the situation of warning and conveying the message.

The interrogative in His words ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾ may be taken in its literal sense. In that case it is one of the rhetorical embellishments that al-Sakkaki (Abu Ya'qub Yusuf ibn Abi Bakr al-Sakkaki) called *sawq al-ma'lum masaq ghayrihi* (driving the known in the manner of other than itself), which the men of letters before him called *tajahul al-arif* (feigned ignorance of one who knows). Al-Sakkaki departed from that designation and said that it occurs in the speech of God, as in His words ﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. Here it serves rebuke, as in the verse of Layla bint Tarif al-Kharijiyya, lamenting her brother al-Walid ibn Tarif al-Shaybani:

"O tree of al-Khabur, why are you in leaf,
as though you did not grieve for the son of Tarif?"

The point of evidence is her words: "as though you did not grieve," and so on.

The rebuke is for their error in thinking they will not suffer the punishment that came upon their likes, to the extent that they seem to regard their disbelievers as better than the disbelievers of the past whose stories have been related. That is, they have no distinguishing quality that places them above suffering what the earlier disbelievers suffered. The meaning is: in your indifference to admonition by the situations of the earlier deniers, you cannot be free of the fact that you lack either of the two things that would reassure you that you will not be struck as they were.

The particle *am* (أمْ) here indicates a transitional change of subject (*idrab intiqali*). What is understood to follow it is an interrogative used for denial. The implied sense is: "Rather, do you not have immunity in the scriptures, so that you would be safe from punishment?"

The pronoun in "your disbelievers" (كُفّارِكم) refers to the people of Makkah, who are themselves the disbelievers. The genitive construction of the word *kuffar* with their pronoun is an explanatory genitive (*idafa bayaniyya*), because the governed noun is a kind of the category of those to whom it is attached. It is therefore taken to mean "min" of explanation (*min al-bayaniyya*). The meaning is: "the disbelievers among you are better than the disbelievers of the past." That is, "Are you, the disbelievers, better than those disbelievers?"

By "superiority" is meant the absence of disbelief; that is, "better in the sight of God" would mean the divine retribution and the claim of a distinction between them and those.

*Al-bara'a* means deliverance and safety from what harms, troubles, or imposes a burden. Here it means deliverance from accountability and punishment.

*Al-zubur* is the plural of *zabur*, which means a book. *Zabur* here carries the sense of *mazbur* (written), so *bara'a* means an immunity written in the books of God that came before.

[Page 211]

The meaning is: "Do you have an immunity written in the scriptures that your disbelievers will not suffer the punishment that befell their likes among the earlier nations?"

"In the scriptures" (فِي الزُّبُرِ) is a qualifier of "immunity" (بَراءَةً), meaning "existing in the scriptures," that is, "written in the pages of the books."

This discourse establishes that deliverance from punishment is presented as alternating between two possibilities: either attaining the divine good indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], or pardon and forgiveness for the evil deeds a person commits, indicated by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Perhaps God looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you."

The meaning is that both of these matters are absent from the addressees, so there is no safety for them from the descent of punishment upon them as it descended upon their likes.

The verse indicates that a punishment is awaited which will befall the polytheists in this world, short of the greater punishment. That is the punishment of hunger mentioned in His words ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10], as has already been explained. It also includes the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr, mentioned in His words ﴿The Day We strike with the greatest assault; indeed We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16].

﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ "Bal" (بَلْ) here is for al-idrab al-intiqali (a transitional shift in discourse), a move from the threat of punishment in this world, as had befallen the nations before them, to the threat of punishment in the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, that perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21], and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater. Therefore He said: ﴿and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ In another verse He said: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127], and in another verse: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgraceful﴾ [Fussilat: 16].

"Al-Sa'ah" (السّاعَةُ, the Hour): in the Qur'an it is a term that has become dominant (ʿilm bi-l-ghalabah) for the Day of Recompense.

"Al-mawʿid" (الْمَوْعِدُ): the time of a promise, and here it refers to a promise of evil, that is, a threat. The construction is an idafah in the sense of the preposition "lam" (li-), meaning "an appointed time for them." This is a general statement of the threat, and then it is followed by what details it, namely ﴿and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ The reason for the conjunction (ʿatf) is that it is intended to be a separate, independent predicate.

"Adhha" (أدْهى): an elative form from "dahahu," meaning he afflicted him with a calamity (dahiyah), i.e., the Hour is more severe in striking with the calamity of eternal abiding in the Fire than the calamity of the punishment of this world by killing and captivity.

"Amarr" (أمَرُّ): meaning more bitter. Bitterness is used metaphorically for the perception of what is disliked, following the manner of likening an intelligible, unseen thing to a sensible, known one.

The name "al-Sa'ah" is repeated in His saying ﴿and the Hour is more calamitous﴾ rather than using a pronoun for it, for the purpose of intensifying the terror, and so that the sentence stands on its own and thus travels as a proverb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verses 47–48:

Page 215
﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾ ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces: "Taste the touch of Saqar!"﴾ This statement is an elaboration of His words, ﴿But the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾ [al-Qamar: 46]. The conjunction of the statement with the particle inna (indeed) serves two purposes: first, emphasis on its declarative content; second, the confirmation of what it implies by way of allusion to the polytheists. Although the speech is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and there is no doubt about that, the polytheists will hear of it and it will spread among them, and they do not believe in the punishment of the Hereafter. So they deserved to have the report emphasized in the sense of allusion, and thus inna is used for both of its purposes, that of emphasis and that of attention.

The expression "the criminals" (al-mujrimin) is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, to attach the description of criminality to them.

Al-dalal (error) is used for the opposite of guidance, and it is also used for loss. Most of the exegetes hold that the intended meaning here is the second. Thus, from Ibn 'Abbas: the intended meaning is loss in the Hereafter, because the apparent sense is that ﴿on the Day they are dragged into the Fire﴾ is a temporal adverb for the state of being ﴿in error and madness﴾, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿On the Day the Quake shakes﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6], ﴿followed by the Second﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 7], ﴿Hearts on that Day will be trembling﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 8], and His saying, ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas: 42]. Therefore it is not fitting that dalal should mean the opposite of guidance.

It is also permissible that ﴿on the Day they are dragged﴾ be an adverb of the existential predicate in the khabar of inna, i.e., they are existing in error and madness on the Day they are dragged into the Fire. The meaning then is: they are in error and madness on the Day of Resurrection.

Su'ur (madness/fire) is the plural of sa'ir, which is the Fire; the plural form is used for sa'ir because it is strong and severe.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 49:

﴿Indeed, We have created everything with measure.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that came as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a closing remark that sums up and confirms what precedes it) to the preceding warning, threat, and call to take heed from what befell the deniers. It is also a preparation (*tawti'a*) for His saying ﴿And Our command is but one [word], like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar: 50], and so on.

The meaning is: We created and did all the actions mentioned, together with their causes, instruments, and means, and We empowered them over those who deserve them, because We created everything with measure. That is, once you know this, take heed that your denial and persistence are similar to what the earlier nations were upon.

The attachment of the report to the particle *inna* (indeed) raises the same point that we made regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾ [al-Qamar: 47]?

Page 217

The root meaning of *khalq* (creation) is bringing a being into existence in a deliberate form. It is therefore literally used for the bringing into existence of essences, and it is used figuratively for the bringing into existence of meanings that resemble essences in distinctness and clarity, as in His saying ﴿and you fabricate a falsehood﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17].

So its use in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have created everything with measure﴾ is a use of the word in both its literal and its figurative sense.

The word *shay'* (thing) means whatever exists, whether substances or accidents. That is, We created all existents, their substances and their accidents, with measure.

*Qadar* (with a fatha on the dal) is a synonym of *qadr* (with a sukun on the dal), and it means the determining and fixing of matters.

The intended meaning is that God's creation of things is accompanied by laws operating in accordance with wisdom. This meaning is repeated in the Qur'an, such as His saying in Surah al-Ra'd ﴿and everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. Among what is included in the generality of "everything" is the creation of Hell for punishment.

He has indicated that recompense is a requirement of wisdom in His saying ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], and His saying ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth, and indeed the Hour is coming, so overlook with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the Knowing﴾ [al-Hijr: 86], and His saying ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38], ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39], ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 40]. You see that these verses and their like follow the mention that all creation is for a wisdom with the mention of the Hour and the Day of Recompense. This is the reason why the verses of warning and punishment in this surah are followed by the concluding statement ﴿Indeed, We have created everything with measure﴾, after His saying ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those [of the past]?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43], and He will say ﴿And We have already destroyed your like﴾ [al-Qamar: 51].

The *ba'* in *bi-qadar* (with measure) denotes accompaniment (*mulabasa*), and the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial complement (*zarf mustaqarr*). It has the status of a second object of the verb *khalaqnahu* (We created it), because it is intended in itself. The aim is not to inform that everything is created by God, since that does not need to be informed of, let alone emphasised. Rather, the aim is to show the meaning of knowledge and wisdom in recompense, as in His saying in Surah al-Ra'd ﴿and everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8].

Page 218

Among what the meaning of *qadar* entails is that every created thing proceeds in accordance with God's knowledge and will, because He is the creator of the origins of things and the one who places powers in them, so that their effects and derivatives emerge from them. Thus He knows that and wills its occurrence. This has been called *qadar* in the technical terminology of the Shari'a, as came in the authentic hadith of Gabriel concerning what constitutes faith: "and you believe in the *qadar*, its good and its evil."

Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayra: "The polytheists of Quraysh came disputing with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about *qadar*, and so there was revealed ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces: Taste the touch of Saqar﴾ [al-Qamar: 48], ﴿Indeed, We have created everything with measure﴾." The narrator of the hadith did not mention the meaning of *qadar* over which the disbelievers of Quraysh disputed, so it remains unspecified. It appears that they disputed in a contentious manner in order to ward off from themselves the rebuke for worshipping idols, as they said ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20]. That is, they argued against the Prophet (ﷺ) by the implication of what he said, that every existing thing is by the *qadar* of God, out of ignorance of the meanings of *qadar*.

'Iyad said in al-Ikmal: "Its apparent meaning is that the intended sense of *qadar* here is God's decree and will, and what His decree has brought about of that, and this is what the context of the story that occasioned the verse indicates." End of quote. Al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: "Linguistically, it may carry the following meanings. First: that *qadar* here means something determined that is neither increased nor decreased, as He said ﴿God has set for everything a measure﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. Second: that the meaning is that it is by His power, as He said ﴿Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyama: 4]. Third: *bi-qadar* means at its time, that is, We determine a time for creating it in which We create it." End of quote.

I say: since the word *qadar* is a generic noun and it occurs governed by a verb connected with the pronoun of *kull shay'* (everything), which signifies generality, that word is general in all its senses. So everything God created, He created with measure. The occasion of revelation does not restrict the generality, and it does not conflict with the placement of this concluding statement. Moreover, the early scholars used to apply the term "occasion of revelation" to anything that the verse indicates, even if the verse preceded what they counted as the occasion.

Know that the verse is explicit that everything God created was in a controlled manner proceeding in accordance with wisdom.

Page 219

As for specifying what God created from among what is not created by Him, such as the actions of servants, according to those who hold that servants create their own actions, like the Mu'tazila, or those who hold the acquisition (*kasb*) of the servant, like the Ash'aris, the verse is no proof against them, because it is possible that the object of the report is the content of "We created it" or the content of "with measure"; and because the generality of "everything" may admit specification; and because it is possible that what is meant by "thing" is something specific. The denial of the verse's authority to establish *qadar*, which is the point of dispute among people, is not refuted by other evidence.

The reality of technical *qadar* is obscure, for the extent to which existent things are affected by God's dispositions, by the causation of their causes, and by the rising of their impediments has not reached the limit of human knowledge, to uncover its obscurities or to know what God has enabled humans to do in executing what God has decreed. The legal and rational evidences require that good deeds and evil deeds are equal in being affected by God's will and the connection of His power when it is connected to something. Therefore, the attribution of the effects of good to God is not different from the attribution of the effect of evil to Him, except as a matter of etiquette with the Creator, which God taught to His servants. Had it not been that both are attributed, in their effect, to God's will, the distinction between the actions of good and the actions of evil in their attribution to God would be akin to the belief of the Magians that good has a god and evil has a god. That is false, given the Prophet's saying (ﷺ) "and you believe in the *qadar*, its good and its evil," and his saying "The Qadariyya are the Magians of this nation," narrated by Abu Dawud with a chain back to Ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

*Kull shay'* (everything) is in the accusative as the object of *khalaqnahu* (We created it), by the construction known as *ishtighal* (the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun, so the noun is placed in the accusative). Its placement before *khalaqnahu* serves to reinforce its meaning by mentioning its explicit noun first and then mentioning its pronoun a second time. This is what requires the shift to *ishtighal* in eloquent Arabic speech, so that the object receives emphasis after the attribution of the verb to its agent has been established by the particle *inna*, which conveys emphasis on the report. Also, so that *bi-qadar* (with measure) is connected to its governing verb, which is *khalaqnahu*, lest it be confused with an adjective of *shay'* if it were said: "Indeed, We created everything with measure," in which case the listener might think that the meaning is "Indeed, We created everything that is measured," and the listener would remain waiting for the predicate of *inna*.

[Page 220]

﴿Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye.﴾

This is conjoined (ʿatf) to His saying ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49], so it falls within the concluding statement (tadhyil, a closing phrase that reinforces the preceding idea). That is, We created everything with knowledge. What is intended is that whatever is suitable for it is known to Us. When its appointed time, which We have prepared, arrives, it comes into being at once, with no prior testing, no deliberation, and no change of plan (bada'). Its verification will come at the end of the commentary on this verse.

The purpose of this is to warn them against the punishment seizing them suddenly in this world when its appointed time is present and its causes and constituent conditions have already come into existence, conditions they do not notice. And in the Hereafter, it is by the arrival of death and then by the establishment of the Hour.

The conjunction of this clause immediately after ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49] indicates that its content follows the content of the clause it is conjoined to, in alerting and in argument, according to the practice of eloquent speakers, who arrange the meanings of speech one after another. So much so that a group of the imams of the Arabic language said so: al-Farra', Tha'lab, al-Rab'i, Qutrub, Hisham, and Abu 'Amr al-Zahid held that the conjunction with "wa" (and) indicates sequence. Ibn Malik said: its most common indication is sequence.

The word "command" (amr) in His saying ﴿Our command﴾ may mean "affair," in which case it refers to the affair appropriate to the context, namely the affair of creation and bringing into being. That is, "the affair of Our creating things."

It may also mean "permission," in which case it refers to the command of bringing into being, which is expressed by the word "Be" (kun). The outcome is the same either way.

On both interpretations, "one" (wahida) is an adjective of an omitted noun that the speech indicates, and it is the predicate concerning "Our command." The sense is: "except one word," namely the word "Be," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya Sin: 82].

What is intended is a metaphor (kinaya) for the swiftest speed possible. That is: Our command is but one word. This applies to the formation of the elements and simple substances, and likewise to the formation of compounds, because the command of bringing into being is directed at them after it has been preceded by creative commands for the bringing into being of their parts. So for each thing composed of them there is a creative command specific to it, which is one word. Thus it becomes clear that God's creative command is one word. This does not conflict with His saying ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [Qaf: 38] and similar verses, for the creation of those things comprised many created things whose number cannot be counted, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Each creation among them occurs by one word, like a glance of the eye, although some created things give rise to other things and effects, and so its creation is reckoned at the bringing into being of its first part.

[Page 221]

The predicate concerning "command," which is masculine, is expressed with "one," which is feminine, because what the command refers to here is the command of subjection (taskhir), which is the word, that is, the word "Be."

His saying ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "Our command," in view of the statement about it that it is one word. That is: the realization of Our will through Our command is like a glance of the eye. It is a comparison in speed of attainment, meaning: Our command is but one word, swift in effect upon what it is directed at, as swift as the glance of the eye.

This comparison in conveying nearness of time is the most eloquent of what has come in the Arabic language, and it is more eloquent than the words of Zuhayr:

So they and the valley of al-Ras are like the hand to the mouth.

It has come in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but like a glance of the eye, or it is nearer﴾ [al-Nahl: 77]. There, "or it is nearer" is added, because the context is a warning against people being taken by surprise by it before they have prepared for it, so it is fitting to exaggerate its nearness. This differs from this verse, where the purpose is to illustrate God's command, and for that, mere alerting suffices, since the listener does not hesitate to believe it.

This verse has conveyed the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of every existing thing, the bringing of existing things into being with wisdom, and their proceeding from will and power.

Al-lamh: a quick look and a stealthy glance. It is said: "he glanced (lamaha) at the sight," and it is said: "he glanced at the lightning," just as it is said: "the lightning flashed (lama'a)." Since the glance of the eye is swifter than the flash of lightning, He, exalted is He, said ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾, as He said in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿except like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Nahl: 77].

[p. 222]

﴿And We have certainly destroyed your like before, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾

He shifted from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab), and the one addressed is the polytheists, since it is evident that they are the intended target of the threat. This is an explicit statement of what was implied in His words ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those? [al-Qamar: 43]﴾. It is thus in the position of a conclusion to His words ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure [al-Qamar: 49]﴾ up to His words ﴿like a glance of the eye [al-Qamar: 50]﴾.

This statement is used to threaten them with destruction and to convey that it will overtake them suddenly, by analogy with the destruction of the earlier nations. This is the purpose for which the statement is emphasized with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and (qad). As for the destruction of those before them, it is well known and does not need emphasis.

You may also take the focus of the emphasis to be the establishment that their destruction occurred because of their polytheism and their denial of the Messengers. The sequence ﴿so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ is an indication that both meanings are intended. The people of Noah remained for ages and did not abandon their polytheism until the flood seized them suddenly. Likewise, 'Ad and Thamud did not believe that the punishment would befall them, and when the punishment came upon them, it came upon them suddenly. The people of Pharaoh went out pursuing Moses and the Children of Israel, confident that they would overtake them, and they drew near to them, thinking they had gained power over them. Then nothing alarmed them except that Allah delivered the Children of Israel, and the sea closed over the others.

The meaning is: just as We destroyed your like, so We will destroy you. And so it was, for when the polytheists arrived at Badr, they were greater in number and equipment, and they were confident that they would rescue their caravan and defeat the Muslims. Abu Jahl said, having urged his horse forward and advanced to the front line, "Today we will take revenge on Muhammad and his companions." But the horses had not turned a single round before they saw their chieftains felled at Badr: Abu Jahl, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and others, seventy men in all. And after that, no standing army was raised for them.

Al-ashya' (the like, the followers) is the plural of shi'ah.

Al-shi'ah is the group that supports the one to whom they are attributed. Its meaning was discussed in His words ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects [al-An'am: 159]﴾ at the end of Surah al-An'am.

[p. 223]

Here, al-ashya' is used for those similar and alike in disbelief, by way of metaphor (isti'arah), since He likens those who have perished to contemporaries who still exist. He made the statement ﴿so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ a consequence of this warning, and a parallel to it has already occurred in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 52:

﴿And everything they did is in the scriptures﴾.

It is permissible that the pronoun in His saying "fa'alūhu" (they did it) refers back to your partisans (ashyā'akum), and the meaning is: We destroyed them with the punishment of this world and prepared for them the punishment of the Hereafter, and so there was recorded in their scrolls of deeds everything they did of disbelief and its branches. Thus the metonymy (kināya) in "fī al-zubur" (in the scriptures) occurs here like a metonymy for its concomitant, which is being reckoned for it afterwards, and for a concomitant that accompanies that, which is punishment after reckoning.

This report is used as an allusion (ta'rīd) addressed to the listeners: that if they expose themselves to what brings destruction upon them in this world, that is not the extent of their punishment, for after it there is a reckoning for it in the Hereafter by which they will be punished. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed for those who have wronged is a punishment short of that﴾ [al-Tur: 47].

It is also permissible in my view that the pronoun refers back to the group in His saying ﴿The multitude will be routed﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], down to "the criminals" in His saying ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾ [al-Qamar: 47], etc. The meaning is: everything the polytheists did of shirk and harm to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the Muslims is counted against them, its punishment prepared for them, because the report about the enumeration of the deeds of past nations has been sufficient without the report about their destruction; so it is more fitting to warn those present against the evil of their deeds.

"Al-Zubur" is the plural of "zabūr," which is a book, derived from "al-zabr" (the writing). The plural "zubur" is used because each one has the book of his own deeds. God, exalted is He, said ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open. "Read your record"﴾ [al-Isra': 13–14], and the verse continues.

The generality of "everything they did" is intended to mean specifically those of their actions for which they will be held accountable in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 54, verse 53:

Page 224
﴿And every small and great thing is recorded.﴾
This is like a concluding remark (tadhyil) to His saying ﴿and everything they have done is in the scriptures﴾ [al-Qamar: 52]. So "every small and great thing" is more general than "everything they have done." The meaning is: every thing, whether insignificant or great, is recorded (mustatar), that is, written down (maskhur), that is, in the knowledge of God the Exalted; that is, God knows all of it and will call to account for it. Thus "mustatar" is a passive participle from "satara," meaning to write lines (sutur). God the Exalted said ﴿and a written book﴾ [al-Tur: 2].

This is like His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but it is in a clear book﴾ [al-An'am: 59], and His saying ﴿Not an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth escapes from Him, nor is there anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear book﴾ [Saba': 3].

So "the small" is used metaphorically for a thing that has no importance, that people do not care about, and whose doer is not held to severe account for it, or is not held to a great accountability for it. "The great" is used metaphorically for its opposite, and it includes what has importance in goodness, what has importance in corruption, and what is below these. That includes the best of righteous deeds and what is below them among righteous deeds; likewise the major sins and grave immoralities and what is below them, such as minor lapses (lamam) and minor sins (saghair).

"Mustatar" is a metonym (kinaya) for God's knowledge of it, and that is a metonym for the recompense for it, in a manner comprising both good tidings and warning.

[p. 225]

Resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani): it follows from what precedes it. When the surah stated that every small and great matter is recorded and that each will be requited, the listener would already know the recompense of the guilty from the verse ﴿Indeed, the guilty are in error and madness﴾ (al-Qamar: 47). The listener's soul was therefore eager to learn the counterpart, the recompense of the God-conscious. This also follows the Qur'an's habit of pairing warning with good news, and the reverse.

Opening this report with the particle inna is for emphasis on it.

The ﴿fi﴾ (in) in ﴿in gardens﴾ is for figurative containment, meaning a strong immersion, like something contained being immersed in its container. The intended sense is that they are in the bliss of gardens and rivers. Gardens and rivers have familiar pleasures: diversion, companionship, conversation, plucking fruits, seeing streams, hearing the sound of running water, the voices of birds, and the colours of swimming creatures.

For this reason ﴿rivers﴾ is coordinated with ﴿gardens﴾. The intention is not to inform that they dwell in gardens, since that would make the later words ﴿in a seat of truth, with a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ superfluous, nor that they are immersed in rivers, since that is not what the listeners would have in mind.

(Nahr) with two fatha vowels is a dialectal variant of (nahr) with fatha then sukun. It is used as a collective noun that admits plurality, as in God's words ﴿Beneath them the rivers flow﴾ (al-A'raf: 43). The phrase ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for ﴿the God-conscious﴾, or in the position of the second predicate of inna.

(Maq'ad) means a place of sitting. Sitting here means dwelling in tranquil settlement, as in God's words ﴿Sit with those who sit﴾ (al-Tawbah: 46).

(Sidq) originally means the correspondence of a report to reality. Then its usages multiplied through metaphor or figurative extension, returning to the sense of something hitting its target in a way that suits the perfection of its kind. The connection of the Name al-Rahman to these considerations is derived from His saying: ﴿And We did not send you, except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

Al-Qur'an (the Qur'an): a term that came to be applied to the verbal revelation that was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), for the purpose of its miraculous challenge (i'jaz) by a single surah from it, and for the worship (ta'abbud) through its wording.
